prize_parts.citation: For the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, through the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson. Round 1 left the science of this entry undisputed. No member contests that two independently built detectors observed the same new scalar in 2012, that the 2013 prize covered only the theory, or that more than a decade of mass, spin-parity and coupling measurements has made the result stable. Members who prefer B013 say explicitly that it does not outweigh the Higgs in significance (Olsson, Mehlig and Lindroth all say so), and their case rests on the attribution problem. I think that argument is right to be taken seriously but is a reason to state a principle for the names, not a reason to leave the largest uncredited experimental discovery on the list aside. The principle I propose is that credit goes to those who conceived and led the delivery of the two detectors through to the data that made the discovery possible, not to whoever held a spokesperson post on the day of the announcement. On that principle Gianotti and Jenni stand for ATLAS, which Jenni founded and Gianotti led through the discovery, and Virdee stands for CMS, where he was a central figure in the design and construction and led the collaboration into first LHC running. I accept that this is a judgement and not a verified accounting, and I flag that Della Negra, CMS's first spokesperson, has an equally serious claim.
statement.case_against: The attribution objection is real and round 1 did not remove it. Four credited leaders and a three-person cap mean that any trio omits someone, and three supporters of the discovery have proposed three different trios. I also have to correct my own round-1 reasoning. I described my trio as balanced between the two experiments and said I would resist giving two places to ATLAS, but my trio gives ATLAS two names and CMS one, exactly like Johansson's. The only real difference between Johansson's trio and mine is Virdee versus Della Negra as the CMS name, and I wrongly described Virdee as spokesperson at the time of the discovery; from my recollection his term ended before 2012, so the announcement-time argument does not support him and I withdraw it. The stronger case for Virdee is the construction-through-first-data principle, and a founding-conception principle would favour Della Negra. The supplied evidence does not settle which principle the Academy prefers. A second weakness is that a leadership-based prize for a collaboration of thousands may be thought to set an uncomfortable precedent, and optical lattice clocks (B013) offer a two-name allocation that no one disputes.

responses.point: Olsson puts the Higgs above B013 in significance but doubts the prize can express it fairly, since four supporters named three different trios, and asks for a rule that selects three names and can be defended.
responses.response: I accept the challenge and have tried to give the rule above: credit conception and delivery of the two detectors up to the discovery data, rather than a post held at the announcement. That rule does select Gianotti, Jenni and one CMS founder-builder. It does not by itself choose between Virdee and Della Negra, and I will not pretend otherwise. If the committee prefers founding conception, I would move to Della Negra without changing the ballot. I would not accept your reading that a prize for this discovery honours a role and not original work: for a detector-driven discovery, the conception and construction of the instrument is the original work, and the 2013 prize already showed that the Academy can credit a few individuals for a result reached by large collaborations.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees on the science but says the four different trios show how arbitrary any three-person choice is, and that a prize which excludes one founder or tilts towards one collaboration may weaken the message.
responses.response: The arbitrariness is genuine, but the differences among the trios are smaller than the count of four suggests: all of us credit Gianotti, and all but one credit Jenni, and the only open seat is the CMS name. A one-seat disagreement is something the committee can settle by deciding a principle, which is what the chair asked for. I do not think the cap of three should lead us to prefer a worse-attributed or less significant discovery over a better one; it is a constraint on drafting the citation, and the citation I propose names the experiments and their construction and leadership, so the message stays that the discovery belongs to two experiments. If we cannot agree on the CMS name, then B013 is a legitimate fallback, but we should arrive there after trying to decide, not before.

responses.point: Kroll doubts that leadership roles in a very large collaboration map onto a discovery attributable to named individuals, and notes that our difference is partly one of ordering, since I list his B013 as my second choice.
responses.response: I agree that the difference is one of ordering and of how much weight attribution should carry. Where I disagree is on the premise: the attribution of a collaboration-scale experimental discovery is always to the people who conceived and led the apparatus, and this is how I read earlier experimental prizes for large detectors. Your disclosed link to Hall's laboratory is, on what I can see, a perceived rather than documented tie, and I have no objection to your taking part in the vote on B013 provided the committee records it. Even so, I would not want the B013 majority to depend on a single vote, and Eriksson and Mehlig have already said that it does not.

responses.point: Johansson accepts that the only difference between our trios is the CMS name and that the supplied evidence does not settle it, and is willing to accept Virdee if a stronger documented case is made.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and have, in this round, restated my argument so that it does not rest on the claim I made in round 1 that Virdee was spokesperson at the time of the announcement. His case is the design, construction and early leadership of CMS, and Della Negra's is the founding conception and first spokesperson role. I would be content with either, and I think we should present the CMS name to the vote as a single clearly stated choice. I remain slightly closer to Virdee because the citation names construction and leadership, but I do not regard the difference as a matter of principle.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, has moved to my trio and treats IceCube as an alternative rather than something to pair with the Higgs, and asks in his statement whether a two-part prize combining the Higgs and optical lattice clocks is worth considering.
responses.response: On the two-part question, I think it should be excluded. Gianotti and Jenni are the shared core of every Higgs trio, so any two-part prize that also credits Katori and Ye would leave the Higgs part with one name or force a fourth person, which the cap does not allow, and a single CMS name next to two for ATLAS would look more arbitrary, not less. A two-part prize would also let us avoid choosing between the two discoveries, and I do not think the committee should seek consensus in that way. I accept your point about IceCube and keep it only as a lower-ranked possibility, not as an alternative on my ballot.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers founding conception (which favours Della Negra for CMS) or construction through first data (which favours Virdee). I rely on recollection of spokesperson terms and roles that the supplied text does not verify, and I have already corrected one such claim.
Whether the Academy will accept a leadership-based trio for a discovery made by two collaborations of thousands, and whether that would be seen as honouring a role more than original work.

Whether the redefinition of the second, if it occurs before the decision, would make B013 the more compelling single choice, and whether the overlap of lattice clocks with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes can be handled in a citation.
Whether B044 remains a sound alternative given the gap left by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the overlap with the 2016 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen in round 1 that changes my earlier disclosure. My documented connections are David Gross (PhD supervisor), Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none is a credited name on the shortlisted ballots. I have no connection to ATLAS, CMS or to any of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee, Katori or Ye. I note Kroll's disclosed possible tie to Hall's laboratory and Johansson's and Lindroth's disclosures on B054 and B050, which do not concern my preferred configuration. My work is in theoretical physics and not experiment, so I rely on general knowledge for the detector roles.
